procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be a lower court in Andhra Pradesh since the High Court heard an appeal.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated September 18, 1963, of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 385 of 1962.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Andhra Pradesh High Court convicted Purna Chandra Rao under s. 342 of the Indian Penal Code but released him under s. 562(1-A) of the Criminal Procedure Code after admonition. The High Court also released A.K. Mallu (the respondent in the other appeal) after admonition under s. 562 (1-A) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Two appeals were filed in the Supreme Court. Criminal Appeal No. 243 of 1964 was filed by Purna Chandra Rao (the person convicted and released with admonition). Criminal Appeal No. 65 of 1964 was filed by A.K. Mallu against the High Court's judgment releasing the respondent (who is the appellant in the other appeal). The appeal of A.K. Mallu was dismissed in default because his advocate withdrew from the case and he was not represented. The Supreme Court dismissed both appeals.

issue.issue_text: Whether the phrase 'any offence under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment' in Section 562(1-A) of the Criminal Procedure Code should be interpreted ejusdem generis with the preceding specific offences (theft, cheating etc.), thereby limiting its application to only offences relating to property.

facts: An accused person was convicted of wrongful confinement under Section 342 of the Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.).
Instead of a sentence, the court released the accused after an admonition under Section 562(1-A) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.).
An appeal was filed arguing that Section 562(1-A) was not applicable because it only pertained to offences concerning property, and wrongful confinement is not a property offence.
law: Section 562(1-A) of the Cr.P.C. applies to convictions for "theft, theft in a building, dishonest misappropriation, cheating or any offence under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment."

The legal doctrine of *ejusdem generis* was invoked, which suggests that when general words follow an enumeration of specific things, the general words are to be construed as applying only to things of the same kind as those specifically mentioned.
application: The Court rejected the argument that the phrase "any offence under the Indian Penal Code..." should be interpreted *ejusdem generis* with the preceding list of offences (theft, cheating, etc.).

The Court's primary reason was that the specific offences like theft and cheating were explicitly mentioned because they are punishable with imprisonment of *more* than two years. It was necessary to list them specifically to bring them within the scope of this provision.
Therefore, the specific offences do not form a 'class' of property offences that limits the subsequent general phrase.
The Court held that the clause "any offence under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment" stands by itself as a separate and independent category.

It reasoned that if the legislature had intended to limit the section's application to only property offences, it could have easily and directly done so by referencing Chapter 17 of the I.P.C., which covers offences against property.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the phrase "any offence under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment" is not limited to property-related offences. It covers all offences under the I.P.C. that meet the two-year punishment threshold, regardless of their nature. Consequently, the provision was correctly applied to the offence of wrongful confinement.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the phrase 'any offence under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment' in Section 562(1-A) of the Criminal Procedure Code should be interpreted ejusdem generis with the preceding specific offences (theft, cheating etc.), thereby limiting its application to only offences relating to property.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (the complainant, represented by Mr. S. C. Aggarwal) argued that Section 562(1-A) is not applicable to an offence of wrongful confinement under Section 342 of the Indian Penal Code.
The reason provided was that Section 562(1-A) is concerned with offences relating to property, and therefore, offences not concerning property cannot be dealt with under this section.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, which the court adopted, was that the section's application is not limited to property offences. If the legislature had intended to limit the operation of Section 562(1-A) to offences against property, it could have easily specified this by mentioning Chapter 17 of the Indian Penal Code, which covers all property-related offences.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The clause 'any offence under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment' in s. 562(1-A) of the Criminal Procedure Code stands by itself and is not to be read ejusdem generis with the specific property-related offences mentioned earlier in the section. Therefore, the section applies to all offences under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment, regardless of whether they relate to property.
obiter: If the legislature had intended to limit the operation of s. 562(1-A) to offences against property, it could have easily done so by referencing Chapter 17 of the Indian Penal Code.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The clause 'any offence under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment' in Section 562(1-A) of the Criminal Procedure Code is not limited to property-related offences. This clause stands by itself as a separate category and is not to be interpreted ejusdem generis with the preceding specific offences like theft and cheating. The specific offences were mentioned only because they are punishable with more than two years' imprisonment and the legislature needed to explicitly include them within the scope of the section.
legal_tests_applied: Ejusdem Generis: The court considered and rejected the application of this rule of statutory interpretation, which would have required the general words ('any offence...') to be construed as being limited to the same class as the preceding specific words (theft, cheating, etc.).
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that the general phrase 'any offence under the Indian Penal Code' should be read ejusdem generis with the preceding specific offences. The court reasoned that the specific offences (theft, cheating, etc.) were mentioned not to create a class of 'property offences', but because they are punishable with more than two years' imprisonment and therefore had to be explicitly listed to be included.

The court found that the clause 'any offence under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment' stands by itself and is a distinct category from the specifically enumerated offences that precede it.
why_respondent_won: The court reasoned that the specific offences like theft were mentioned because their punishment exceeds two years, thus making it necessary to list them separately to bring them within the section's ambit, which otherwise covers all offences punishable with not more than two years.

The court reasoned that if the legislature had intended to limit the section's application to only property offences, it could have easily and directly done so by referencing Chapter 17 of the Indian Penal Code, which contains all offences against property. The absence of such a reference indicates a broader legislative intent.
